label: Projective and Birational Geometry
notes: Open the chapter. Affine space is missing its points at infinity, and many theorems become clean only after we add them. The deck follows printed pages 87 through 100 and introduces projective space, projective varieties and homogeneous ideals, rational and birational maps, and the way blow-ups resolve the indeterminacy these maps carry.

label: Projective Space
notes: Construct projective space as lines through the origin, or equivalently as affine space completed by a hyperplane at infinity. Homogeneous coordinates are defined only up to scaling, so only homogeneous polynomials have well-defined zero sets. This completion is what makes intersection theory uniform: parallel lines now meet, and Bezout's theorem holds without exceptions.

label: Projective Varieties
notes: Define projective varieties as zero sets of homogeneous ideals in projective space. They are covered by affine pieces, the standard charts, so local questions reduce to the affine theory already developed. Projective varieties are the natural compact arena for algebraic geometry, where degree and intersection behave far better than in the affine world.

label: Rational and Birational Maps
notes: Introduce rational maps, defined by ratios of homogeneous polynomials away from a locus where they break down. A birational map has a rational inverse, making two varieties birationally equivalent: isomorphic on dense open sets. Birational classification is coarser than isomorphism and is the central organizing problem of higher algebraic geometry.

label: Blow-ups
notes: Resolve the indeterminacy of rational maps with the blow-up, which replaces a point by the projective space of directions through it. Blowing up separates branches and turns many rational maps into genuine morphisms. This single construction underlies resolution of singularities and the birational surgery that classifies surfaces and beyond.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Projective space completes affine space with points at infinity, projective varieties come from homogeneous ideals, rational and birational maps relax isomorphism to agreement on dense opens, and blow-ups tame their indeterminacy. These tools set the stage for tangent spaces, dimension, and the famous count of lines on a cubic surface.
